questions.question: Why does EU consumer law matter to influencers who regularly advertise or sell products?

gold_answer.summary: Regular commercial activity can make an influencer a trader subject to consumer-protection obligations.
key_points: regular commercial activity can trigger trader status

gold_quotations.quote: When you monetize your content, whether you advertise goods and products on your social media channels or sell them on your personal websites, you are considered a trader by the law.
supports: regular commercial activity can trigger trader status

gold_quotations.quote: In the European Union, traders have a lot of responsibilities, and it doesn't matter if you're a one person business or a big tech company - these obligations will be the same.
supports: regular commercial activity can trigger trader status

claim_evidence_mapping.claim: regular commercial activity can trigger trader status

questions.question: Does EU consumer protection apply only to large companies?

gold_answer.summary: No. The materials explain that trader obligations can apply to one-person businesses as well as large companies.
key_points: consumer obligations are not limited to large companies

gold_quotations.quote: This is why it is important to understand the laws that apply to selling goods as well as providing services, and highlighting some of the most important obligations that you need to keep in mind as a trader.

gold_quotations.quote: For instance, if you are selling your merchandise on social media platforms as a trader, this obligation will apply to you as well.

questions.question: Is the Influencer Legal Hub presented as an exhaustive statement of every law that can apply to influencers?

gold_answer.summary: No. The Hub presents selected important EU rules and explains that other national, media and self-regulatory rules can also matter.

gold_answer.legal_caution: Do not treat the Hub as a complete substitute for jurisdiction-specific legal advice.

questions.question: What is the main EU consumer-law concept used in the Hub to determine whether influencer consumer rules apply?

gold_answer.summary: The key concept is whether the influencer acts as a 'trader' in commercial practices.
key_points: trader status is central to the UCPD framework

gold_quotations.quote: Meanwhile, we can focus on the legal standards of the main consumer law that applies to advertising - that's the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive (UCPD).
supports: trader status is central to the UCPD framework

gold_quotations.quote: In the eyes of European law, when someone (whether a person or a company) has commercial activities that occur on a regular basis and for profit, consumer protection applies.
supports: trader status is central to the UCPD framework

claim_evidence_mapping.claim: trader status is central to the UCPD framework

questions.question: What three broad elements does the Hub describe for trader status?

gold_answer.summary: The brief discusses revenue through content monetisation, commercial practices towards consumers, and acting in connection with a trade, business, craft or profession.

gold_quotations.quote: The UCPD defines a 'trader' as 'any natural or legal person who, in commercial practices covered by this Directive, is acting for purposes relating to his trade, business, craft or profession and anyone acting in the name of or on behalf of a trader'.
**You need to be acting in connection to your trade, business, craft or profession, meaning that you're acting as a professional. **

questions.question: Can an influencer be a trader without being incorporated as a company?

gold_answer.summary: Yes. The brief expressly discusses natural persons and one-person businesses, including people who have not registered a business.

gold_quotations.quote: 'Commercial activities' are all supposed to bring you revenue, so whether you're what lawyers would call a 'natural person', a one-person business (like a freelancer) or a registered company, you are considered a 'Trader' and the UCPD applies.

The trader definition is no simple definition, because it needs to include businesses from all possible industries and of all possible categories - and as we have seen, even individuals who have not registered a business with a local Chamber of Commerce.

questions.question: Does selling eight items online automatically make someone a trader under Kamenova?

gold_answer.summary: No. The brief says the Kamenova criteria are not a mechanical checklist and that selling eight items did not automatically establish trader status.
key_points: eight sales alone were not automatically decisive

gold_quotations.quote: In its ruling, the Court ended up saying that just because this Bulgarian citizen wanted to sell eight products on an online platform, it did not automatically make her a trader.
supports: eight sales alone were not automatically decisive

gold_quotations.quote: For instance, if you are selling your merchandise on social media platforms as a trader, this obligation will apply to you as well.
supports: eight sales alone were not automatically decisive

questions.question: What kinds of factors did the Kamenova case identify as potentially relevant to trader status?

gold_answer.summary: Relevant factors include organisation of sales, profit intention, expertise, legal status, VAT, remuneration or incentives, resale activity, product type/value and concentration of the offer.
key_points: VAT is one factor, not a standalone test

gold_quotations.quote: In this case, a Bulgarian citizen had published a total of eight product ads on olx.bg, and the question the Court had to answer was whether she qualified as a trader or not.
supports: VAT is one factor, not a standalone test

gold_quotations.quote: According to the Consumer Sales Directive updated in 2019, a 'sales contract' is a transaction where the trader agrees to deliver a product and transfer ownership to a consumer, and the consumer agrees to pay a price.
supports: VAT is one factor, not a standalone test
